vignette:
It was a Tuesday evening in late spring when the police pulled Samir over. They had been cycling home from a community meeting, the mild air pleasant against their skin, when a cruiser’s lights flared behind them. Samir, a 46-year-old software engineer who had lived in the same neighborhood for fifteen years, did not understand why they were being stopped. They had done nothing wrong. The officers were out of the car before Samir could speak, shouting, hands reaching. The memory that remained was not a story but a series of fragments—the crack of their own skull against the asphalt, the weight of a knee on their spine, the sound of their own voice saying please over and over. What stayed with them most was not a clear image but the full, suffocating emotional force of that moment, arriving without warning and without a picture attached. They could not tell a coherent story of what happened, even to themselves; whenever they tried, they found themselves pushing the memory away before they could reach the end.

In the months that followed, Samir discovered that certain moments could dismantle them. Feeling happy or relaxed was the worst. A quiet afternoon, a good meal, a laugh with their spouse—and then, without transition, the emotional weight of that Tuesday evening would collapse onto them, unbidden and imageless. They began to watch other people closely for signs that they might harm, scanning faces in the grocery store, on the train, in the conference room at work. They had come to believe that you could never know who would harm you, and that their own beliefs about how the world worked had been completely destroyed. Every confrontation, even a mild disagreement with a colleague about a code review, felt like a potential escalation. The world felt full of hidden threats, and Samir was certain that others could see what had happened to them just by looking at them, as though the trauma was written on their skin.

The causal connections tightened into a loop that Samir could not escape. Each time a trigger appeared—a cyclist passing them on the street, a raised voice in a meeting—the memory threatened to surface, and Samir pushed it away before it could complete itself. That incomplete, fragmented memory left them feeling exposed and unsafe, which only deepened their belief that harm was everywhere. And that belief, in turn, made them more vigilant, more watchful, more likely to interpret a stranger’s glance as a threat. Samir had developed a habit of choosing where to sit based on how safe or protected they felt—always with their back to a wall, always with a clear view of the exits. Their body reacted before their mind could catch up: a racing heart, a knot in their stomach, a tremor in their hands. At work, they had started taking the stairs instead of the elevator, because the enclosed space felt too much like the back of the cruiser. Their spouse had noticed that Samir no longer wanted to go for walks after dinner, that they flinched at the sound of a siren on the television.

What finally brought Samir to seek help was a moment at their desk. They had been feeling unusually calm, focused on a debugging problem, and then a colleague cycled past the window on the way to the bike rack. The image was brief, almost incidental, but it triggered a cascade of physical reactivity so intense that Samir had to excuse themselves to the bathroom, where they sat on the floor, shaking, unable to form a single clear thought about why. They were tired of being dismantled by happiness, tired of scanning every room for danger, tired of the fragmented, incomplete memories that haunted them without ever telling a full story. They were afraid that if they did not find a way to break the cycle, they would lose the parts of their life they still valued—their work, their marriage, their ability to feel safe in their own skin.
